description: Government tools for market failure: taxes, subsidies, regulation and state provision, and why intervention may fail.
content_html:
Why Governments Step In

Markets are a powerful way to allocate resources, but the previous lessons showed that they can fail. When producers or consumers generate externalities, or when public and merit goods are left to the market alone, resources end up misallocated — too much of some things, too little of others. Governments intervene to push the economy closer to the outcome that is best for society as a whole. The question is not just whether to intervene, but which tool to use and at what scale.

Key Fact

The four main tools of government intervention are: indirect taxes, subsidies, regulation and legislation, and direct state provision. Each works differently and suits different types of market failure.

Indirect Taxes to Reduce Negative Externalities

When a firm or consumer creates a negative externality — pollution, congestion, health damage — the social cost of their activity is higher than the private cost they actually pay. They therefore do too much of it. An indirect tax raises the price of the harmful good so that it better reflects the true social cost. The chain of reasoning is: tax raises price → higher price reduces quantity demanded → consumption falls towards the socially optimal level.

A familiar example is the tax on petrol and diesel. Burning fossil fuels creates carbon emissions that contribute to air pollution and climate change — external costs borne by the whole of society. By raising the pump price with fuel duty, the government aims to reduce the quantity of fuel consumed and encourage motorists to switch to cleaner alternatives or use public transport more often. The tax also raises revenue that can, in principle, be used to repair the damage caused or invest in cleaner infrastructure.

Similarly, tobacco and alcohol duties are designed to reduce consumption of goods whose overuse imposes costs on the NHS and on families. Students often call these “sin taxes.” From an economics perspective, the aim is to shift quantity consumed towards the level the market would produce if all social costs were internalised.

An indirect tax only works well if demand is price elastic. If consumers are heavily addicted to a product — cigarettes, for example — the price elasticity of demand (PED) is very low (inelastic), so a price rise causes only a small fall in consumption. The tax mainly transfers money from consumers to the government rather than solving the externality. There is also a regressive dimension: lower-income households spend a larger proportion of their income on taxed goods, so indirect taxes can widen inequality.

Subsidies to Encourage Positive Externalities

Positive externalities work in the opposite direction. When consumption or production creates benefits for third parties — education raises the skill of the whole workforce; vaccination reduces the spread of disease to those not vaccinated — the private benefit to the individual is less than the social benefit. The market left alone produces too little of these goods. A subsidy reduces the cost of producing or consuming the good, encouraging more of it.

Consider free NHS vaccinations. The private benefit to the person vaccinated is protection from illness. The external benefit is that they also cannot pass the disease on to others — a benefit to society that the individual does not capture in their private calculation. Without a subsidy (or free provision), some people would choose not to pay for vaccination, meaning herd immunity is not reached. By providing vaccinations at zero cost, the government increases uptake towards the socially optimal level.

Subsidies are also used for public transport, home insulation, and apprenticeship programmes. In each case, the private market underproduces because providers cannot capture all the social benefit their activity creates. The subsidy closes that gap by making production cheaper or consumption less costly.

Key Fact

A subsidy lowers the private cost — raising quantity supplied or demanded — moving output towards the socially optimal level. It is the counterpart to an indirect tax, used where positive externalities cause the market to underproduce.

Regulation and Legislation

Regulation uses legal rules rather than price signals to change behaviour. Governments can set maximum permitted levels of pollution, ban harmful substances, require seatbelts, or make school attendance compulsory. Unlike taxes or subsidies, regulation does not rely on market forces — it simply draws a line and enforces it.

Environmental regulation is a prominent example. Factory emissions limits require firms to install cleaner technology or reduce output. Road transport regulations — MOT requirements, emissions standards for new vehicles — reduce the external cost imposed on those who breathe polluted air. Regulation tends to be most effective when the externality is severe, when the government can monitor compliance cheaply, and when there are no easy workarounds.

Regulation can also address information failure. Food labelling laws, for example, require producers to disclose ingredients and nutritional content. This corrects the asymmetry of information between producers (who know exactly what is in a product) and consumers (who do not). When consumers are better informed, they can make choices that reflect the true costs and benefits of consumption.

Taxes work through incentives: firms can still pollute if they are willing to pay. Regulation draws a hard limit. Taxes are economically efficient — the firm with the lowest abatement cost will cut emissions most — but hard to set at exactly the right level. Regulation gives certainty about the maximum harm permitted, but can be inflexible (a firm that could cut pollution cheaply gets the same limit as one for which it is very expensive). In practice, most governments use both: carbon pricing (a tax) alongside emission standards (regulation).

State Provision and Information Campaigns

Some goods suffer such severe market failure that taxes and subsidies are insufficient. State provision means the government provides the good itself — funded through taxation — rather than leaving it to private suppliers. Public goods, which are non-excludable and non-rival (street lighting, national defence), would not be provided at all by the market because of the free-rider problem. The government therefore provides them directly. Merit goods such as education and healthcare are provided free at point of use to ensure adequate consumption, even if partial private markets also exist.

Information provision is a lighter touch. Rather than regulating or taxing, the government can simply improve consumers’ knowledge. Public health campaigns about smoking, obesity, and alcohol are examples. If people underestimate the risks — because of information failure — then better information can shift their choices without coercion. Anti-smoking campaigns, for instance, provide data on health consequences and display graphic warnings on packaging. Over time, such campaigns have contributed to a significant fall in smoking rates in the UK.

Government Failure and Unintended Consequences

Intervention is not guaranteed to improve outcomes. Government failure occurs when the cure is worse than the disease — or at least no better. There are several reasons this can happen.

First, the government may lack sufficient information. Setting the right tax rate on pollution requires knowing the exact monetary value of the external cost, which is very difficult to measure accurately. A tax that is too low does not solve the problem; a tax that is too high reduces economic activity more than is justified.

Second, there can be unintended consequences. A sugar tax on fizzy drinks might lead consumers to switch to other high-calorie products not covered by the tax, so total calorie intake barely changes. A ban on one type of drug can shift consumption to a different, possibly more dangerous substitute. Higher fuel taxes can make it harder for low-income families in rural areas — who have no alternative to driving — to afford basic transport.

Third, regulation can be captured by the industries it is meant to control. If firms lobby effectively, regulations may be weakened to the point where they do little to correct the externality. This is sometimes called “regulatory capture.”

The existence of government failure does not mean intervention is always wrong — it means governments must weigh the cost of market failure against the cost of intervention failing. The right policy depends on the size of the externality, the availability of information, the elasticity of demand and supply, and how easy it is to enforce the intervention.
exam_tip_html: This topic is ideal for “Evaluate” questions because every intervention has trade-offs. When the command word is Evaluate, go beyond listing pros and cons — make a supported judgement. The strength of your conclusion depends on the context: a high indirect tax works well when demand is price elastic (so consumption falls significantly) but poorly when demand is inelastic (so it mainly just raises prices and hits poorer households hardest). Always ask: “it depends on…” and then state exactly what it depends on — elasticity, size of the externality, cost of enforcement, time period. A common mistake is writing only about indirect taxes and ignoring regulation, subsidies, and state provision; show the examiner you know the full toolkit.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Governments correct market failure with four main tools: indirect taxes (to reduce negative externalities), subsidies (to encourage positive externalities), regulation (to set hard limits on harmful behaviour), and state provision (for public and merit goods that the market undersupplies).
  • Each tool has strengths and weaknesses; effectiveness depends on elasticity, information quality, and enforcement costs — a well-set tax can internalise an externality efficiently, but a badly calibrated one can create new problems.
  • Government failure is a real risk: information gaps, unintended consequences, and regulatory capture can mean intervention fails to improve resource allocation, or even makes it worse.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is an example of government using an indirect tax to correct a negative externality?
A) The government pays a subsidy to electric car manufacturers
B) The government imposes fuel duty on petrol and diesel
C) The government provides free vaccinations to the public
D) The government sets a minimum wage in the labour market
practice_questions.marks: B) The government imposes fuel duty on petrol and diesel [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: A government imposes a new pollution tax on a factory. Before the tax, the factory produced 10,000 units of output per year. After the tax, it produces 8,500 units. Calculate the percentage change in output as a result of the tax.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for the correct method: percentage change = (new value − original value) ÷ original value × 100 = (8,500 − 10,000) ÷ 10,000 × 100; 1 mark for the correct answer of −15% (a fall of 15%).

practice_questions.text: Explain why a subsidy on apprenticeship training may help to correct a positive externality in the labour market.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the positive externality: trained workers benefit not only the firm that trains them but also society as a whole (e.g. higher productivity, lower unemployment); 1 mark for explaining the market failure: because firms cannot capture all the social benefit, they invest in training less than is socially optimal; 1 mark for linking to the subsidy: a subsidy lowers the cost of providing training, encouraging firms to offer more apprenticeships, moving output towards the socially optimal level.

practice_questions.text: A local council introduces a congestion charge of £15 per day for drivers entering the city centre. Explain how this policy might correct the negative externality caused by road congestion.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the negative externality: traffic congestion imposes external costs on other road users (delays), on local residents (pollution, noise), and on emergency services; 1 mark for explaining the mechanism: the charge raises the private cost of driving to better reflect the social cost, acting like an indirect tax; 1 mark for the effect: drivers who value the journey at less than £15 will switch to public transport or travel at different times, reducing congestion; 1 mark for development: the effectiveness depends on the price elasticity of demand for car travel — if demand is inelastic, relatively few drivers will switch and the externality persists, though the charge still raises revenue.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a government could use regulation to reduce the negative externalities caused by a factory that discharges chemical waste into a river.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6): Detailed chain of reasoning explaining how regulation sets a legal limit on emissions, the mechanism by which this changes the firm's behaviour (threat of fines forces investment in cleaner technology or output reduction), and the wider effect on social costs. Evaluates at least one limitation (e.g. cost of monitoring and enforcement; risk of regulatory capture; the firm may relocate to avoid the regulation). Chain is explicit and well-developed.

Secure (3–4): Clear explanation of how regulation works (legal limit backed by penalties), with a relevant effect on the firm's behaviour. Some attempt to consider a limitation, though development may be incomplete.

Developing (2): Some understanding that regulation involves rules, but the mechanism linking the rule to a reduction in external costs is vague. Limited or no evaluation.

Emerging (1): Basic statement that the government could make rules, with no further development.

practice_questions.text: 'Indirect taxes are the most effective way for a government to correct market failure.' Evaluate this view.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support (indirect taxes are effective):
• An indirect tax directly raises the price of the good causing the externality, reducing consumption through the price mechanism — it works with market forces rather than against them.
• It generates government revenue, which can be recycled into repairing damage (e.g. road improvements, NHS spending) or reducing other distortionary taxes.
• Taxes are economically efficient: firms and consumers with low-cost ways to reduce harmful behaviour will do so first, minimising the total cost to the economy.
• Examples: fuel duty, tobacco duty, and alcohol taxes have all contributed to long-run falls in consumption of these goods.

Arguments against (other tools may be more effective, or taxes may fail):
• Indirect taxes rely on demand being price elastic. Where demand is inelastic — as with cigarettes for addicted smokers — the tax mainly redistributes income from consumers to the government rather than solving the externality.
• Indirect taxes are regressive: lower-income households pay a larger share of their income, potentially increasing inequality even as the externality is partly corrected.
• Regulation offers a harder ceiling on harm. Emission standards, for example, guarantee a maximum pollution level regardless of elasticity. The government cannot guarantee the level of reduction from a tax alone.
• Subsidies and state provision better address positive externalities and public goods, which taxes cannot solve.
• Government failure: setting the tax at exactly the right level requires information about the monetary value of the external cost, which is difficult to measure — an incorrectly calibrated tax may under-correct or over-correct.

Judgement:
The effectiveness of indirect taxes depends on the type of market failure. For negative externalities where demand is elastic (e.g. congestion charging where motorists have alternatives), taxes are arguably the most efficient tool. But for public goods, they are irrelevant — state provision is required. For merit goods, subsidies or regulation may be more targeted. An evaluation that concludes 'it depends on the type of externality, the elasticity of demand, and the government's ability to set the right rate' will reach the top band.

Mastering (10–12): Balanced, developed argument with clear chains of reasoning on both sides; a specific and supported judgement that identifies the conditions under which taxes are and are not the most effective tool.

Secure (7–9): Clear points on both sides with some development; a conclusion that leans one way, though support may be partially developed.

Developing (4–6): Some relevant points but limited development; may list pros and cons without a clear chain; conclusion present but weakly supported.

Emerging (1–3): A few basic points; little balance or development; no real judgement.

knowledge_checks.q: What is the main purpose of an indirect tax on a good with a negative externality?
options: To raise the private cost so it better reflects the social cost
To increase consumption of the good
To subsidise producers of cleaner alternatives

knowledge_checks.q: Which government policy tool is best suited to providing a pure public good such as national defence?
A subsidy reduces the cost of producing or consuming a good, moving output towards the _____ optimal level.
Government _____ occurs when intervention to correct market failure makes the situation worse or creates new inefficiencies.
Match each government intervention to its primary purpose:
right: Reduce a negative externality by raising private costs
Encourage a positive externality by lowering private costs
Set a legal ceiling on harmful behaviour backed by penalties

flashcard_questions.q: What is an indirect tax designed to do when a good has a negative externality?
flashcard_questions.a: Raise its price so private cost better reflects the full social cost, reducing consumption.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does a high indirect tax on cigarettes often fail to cut consumption significantly?
flashcard_questions.a: Demand is price inelastic — addicted smokers are unresponsive to price rises.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a subsidy in economics?
flashcard_questions.a: A government payment that lowers the cost of producing or consuming a good, encouraging greater output.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does the market underproduce goods with positive externalities?
flashcard_questions.a: The private benefit is less than the social benefit, so individuals consume less than is socially optimal.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one example of a subsidy used to correct a positive externality.
flashcard_questions.a: Free NHS vaccinations, which raise uptake towards the level needed for herd immunity.

flashcard_questions.q: How does regulation differ from a tax as a way of correcting a negative externality?
flashcard_questions.a: Regulation sets a hard legal limit on harmful behaviour; a tax uses price incentives to reduce it.

flashcard_questions.q: What does state provision mean in the context of correcting market failure?
flashcard_questions.a: The government directly supplies a good — funded by taxation — rather than leaving it to private markets.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does the government provide public goods such as street lighting directly?
flashcard_questions.a: Because of the free-rider problem — private firms cannot charge users, so the market will not supply them.

flashcard_questions.q: Government failure: what happens when the information needed to set a pollution tax is inaccurate?
flashcard_questions.a: The tax may be set too low (externality persists) or too high (too much economic activity is reduced).

flashcard_questions.q: What is an unintended consequence of a sugar tax on fizzy drinks?
flashcard_questions.a: Consumers may switch to other high-calorie products not covered by the tax, so health outcomes barely improve.

flashcard_questions.q: How does information provision correct market failure caused by information failure?
flashcard_questions.a: It gives consumers accurate data, enabling choices that reflect the true costs and benefits.

flashcard_questions.q: When is an indirect tax most effective at reducing a negative externality?
flashcard_questions.a: When demand is price elastic — so a price rise causes a large fall in quantity consumed.
When an industry successfully lobbies to weaken the regulations designed to control it.

glossary_terms.definition: A cost or benefit that falls on a third party who is not directly involved in the transaction.
A tax placed on goods or services rather than directly on income; it raises the price paid by consumers and is used to reduce consumption of goods with negative externalities.
A measure of how sensitive quantity demanded is to a change in price; PED = percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price.
A payment by the government to producers or consumers to lower costs and encourage greater output or consumption of a good with positive externalities.
Rules imposed by the government or a regulatory body that require or prohibit certain actions, backed by legal penalties.
The direct supply of goods or services by the government, typically where the market undersupplies or fails to supply at all.
When government intervention to correct market failure makes the situation worse or creates new inefficiencies, rather than improving resource allocation.
